Decapolis
dih-KAP-uh-lis
proper noun (place)
Greek Dekapolis, "ten cities"; a region of ten Greek cities east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee.

See also: Decapolis

Biblical Definition

The Decapolis ("ten cities") was a region of largely Gentile, Greek-speaking cities east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee, where the gospel of Christ began to reach beyond the Jews even in the days of His earthly ministry. Great multitudes from the Decapolis followed Jesus early on (Matt 4:25). It was in the country of the Gadarenes, within this region, that the Lord healed the man possessed by a legion of demons; and when the man begged to follow Him, Jesus sent him home as a missionary: "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee... And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel" (Mark 5:19-20). Later the Lord passed through the Decapolis, healed a deaf man with a speech impediment (Mark 7:31-37), and fed the four thousand in that region. The Decapolis stands in the dictionary as a region of early Gentile-ward gospel advance, a witness that the saving works of Christ were proclaimed among the Greek cities even before the great commission, that a delivered demoniac became the first herald of Christ to a Gentile people, and that the mercy of the Savior was never meant to be confined to Israel alone.

Webster 1828 Definition

A region of ten Greek cities east of the Sea of Galilee where the healed Gadarene demoniac published Christ (Mark 5:20) and Jesus healed and fed multitudes; a place of early Gentile-ward gospel advance.

DECAPOLIS, proper noun. "Ten cities"; a region of Greek cities east of the Sea of Galilee.

Largely Gentile and Greek-speaking.

From which great multitudes followed Jesus (Matt 4:25).

Where the healed Gadarene demoniac published Christ (Mark 5:19-20).

Where Jesus healed a deaf man and fed the four thousand (Mark 7:31-37).

Key Scripture

Mark 5:20 — "And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel."

Matt 4:25 — "And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and from Decapolis, and from Jerusalem, and from Judaea, and from beyond Jordan."

Mark 7:31 — "And again, departing from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, he came unto the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis."

Mark 7:37 — "And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well..."

Modern Corruption

Decapolis needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the early reach of Christ's mercy and gospel beyond Israel to the Gentile world.

expand to see more

Narrow-mercy correction. Some imagine the mercy of Christ confined to the Jews until after His resurrection. The Decapolis tells otherwise: there the Lord cast out a legion, healed the deaf, and fed the multitude, and a delivered Gentile-region man became the first to publish His works among his own people. The dictionary holds that the compassion of Christ overflowed the borders of Israel even in His earthly ministry, a foretaste of the gospel that would go to all nations.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the herald's commission given to the rescued. The healed demoniac wished to stay with Jesus, but the Lord sent him to tell his friends "how great things the Lord hath done for thee." The dictionary commends this pattern: those whom Christ has delivered are sent back to their own people as witnesses, and the simple testimony of a changed life — what great things the Lord has done — carries the gospel where the rescued can go and others cannot.
